review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

review_text_raw:
[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Final Verdict: Buy! Spoiler-Free Review.[/h1]

This game took me about 3.5 hours to complete on my first playthrough (there are alternate endings available). I tried to read every bit of text and watch every video / photo involved. This game does disappoint as a horror game, but as a mystery thriller, it is excellent. 

This is not a mixed or alternate reality game where you search the web for answers or give your e-mail. The experience is pretty linear, although you can make different choices, the experience goes pretty much through the same set of main events (except for the endings which can vary). You will be looking through videos, photos, Jabbr (facebook), Spark (Tinder), the web (in-game only browser), phone numbers, and e-mails. You simply have to find the relevant information to unlock passcodes or find connections to progress the story. 

You will also have dialogue choices. Some of those choices can have an impact on the story, for example, having more trust with that person and thus giving you a different ending. The story starts out very strong when it is a mystery about what happened to the missing woman, Anna. Even the creepy stuff is exciting at first when you see the distorted videos and the atmosphere leaves things to the imagination. The dialogue between characters is well-written. 

Unfortunately, when you find out the mystery then the horror elements become more silly than scary. I actually just started to troll everybody, trying to get the worst possible ending. There was some real tension at the start and middle of this game, but towards the end, I really didn't feel any connection to any of the characters or "the danger" involved.

That's a shame because this is a very polished experience. The actors all did a nice job overall (sure some of the acting could have been better, but it's better than what is in most games). The mystery sequences where you're sleuthing and trying to find the truth all work extremely well. It's just too bad it ends in a whimper instead of a bang.

[b]Rate 7/10. I still recommend this. With a better ending(s), this could have been something very special. Good overall, but should have been great![/b]

review_text_raw:
A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

review_text_raw:
I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. 

[h3] Anna [/h3]
They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. 

[h3] Greg [/h3]
People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. 

[h3] Ashley [/h3]
THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler].

[h3] Everyone else [/h3]
Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job.

[h3] Simulacra [/h3]
Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I dunno, I just wanted one last big scare, or something that felt satisfying after all that buildup. Then I saw it, and I thought, that's it?

[h2] Story [/h2]
In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference. 

Some aspects were rewarding. I liked getting to put that one workplace creep in his place. I liked when I got her a new job in that one playthrough.

I think the main issues with the story were already discussed in the characters section. I don't think the payoff was satisfying. I think I see what they are going for, with the good ending that is. You have to become a master manipulator to take down the manipulator, I do like that. Again, I just felt like the final boss was an absolute joke. I thought it was fake, there was another boss behind the boss, or something. I think the plot excels in relationship drama and just making terrible people act terrible. It's guilty pleasure level entertaining. It gets lost in the big ideas and trying to be bigger than it actually is. I think if it had stuck to a nitty gritty found phone horror game, with people as its worst enemy, it would've stuck the landing a bit more.

[h2] Theme [/h2]
Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. But maybe...maybe that's the real point. We can look back at a preinternet time and recognize that certain things were better back then. But the fact of the matter is, that world doesn't exist anymore. 

Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna. 

[h1] Wait, didn't you recommend this game? I'm confused [/h1]
Yes. I do.

I think it's fun. Fun like watching the Scream franchise. Fun like a haunted hayride sponsored by a high school, where you know things are corny, but you know what, for those couple of times they made you jump, it was worth spending a couple bucks for a ride. Just wait for a Steam sale and get it for like a dollar like I did. This was a really well spent dollar.

review_text_raw:
As I write this I'm not sure whether or not I will be recommending it or not... I certainly appreciate it for doing something new, and on that level I recommend playing it just so that original ideas get more light brought onto them in a gaming market saturated by copy and pastes of the same MMO or the same First Person Shooter or the same RPG with unnecessary level up mechanics.

That being said, I think it forgets that the game is inherently creepy without needing to throw jumpscares at you. Every time a jumpscare happened I burst into laughter and any amount of tension that had built up was now vanished. Because when it happens, you've been given a signal that now things are going back to normal. The suspense is suddenly lost as you go back to goofing around on someone else's phone.

The game is best described as a cross between Her Story and Orwell but without coming together as nicely as either. I thought that the ending was great, but the path to get there felt a bit too linear. I had figured out how I could get information and obtained information, and then was stuck in a text conversation about how I was going to obtain said information. The freedom in exploration that I was given didn't match some of the conversations that needed to happen. Though there was one bit that was quite nice in that you could figure something out incredibly early without it feeling like you were being roadblocked until another conversation happened.

All in all it's definitely worth checking out, but Her Story and Orwell did it better.

review_text_raw:
[h1] - Is this Anna?
 - No, This Is Patrick! [/h1]
I’m really shocked how such a “small” yet “simple” game could be such a banger, it is great, interesting and awesome. Full playthrough took me about 6 hours and it was amazing – the gameplay is very simple, you just go through the found smartphone, but it is so fresh and original that you can’t stop diving deeper into the gameplay and story; the story itself is very catchy and it mediates between a cool (and I mean really cool) horror story and kind of detective, where you need to solve smart, interesting puzzles. But here are the important things: it does not feel like just a solving puzzles, you literally investigating a very strange and creepy case, everything feels so alive and real (characters, surfing through the mail, chatting, etc.) and most important that it creates a strong feeling that the choices matter – crazy plot twists, extreme tension, and the sense of realism; about horror –  it’s just perfect, not very much of it but it is placed at the right moments and always hits at the right time. 
It definitely gives me some cool vibes that are crazy mix between “laptop” horror movies (Open Windows, Unfriend) and oldschool “teenager” horrors series (Tales From The Crypt, Are You Afraid Of The Dark?). One of the best games I’ve played for a long time and definitely a hidden gem. 
Do I recommend this game? Strongly recommend.

!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative as[i][/i]shole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. And the nice thing is that the developers even implemented a fast-forward feature for repeat playthroughs so you can get through the text conversations faster, which was much appreciated. So yeah, if you want a modern example of how an FMV game can work and you can stomach some stilted acting and don’t mind the presence of generally dislikable characters, I’d recommend these games, they’re a fun little distraction.

A psychological horror/mystery about invading others privacy and cyberstalking?  Talk about checking all my boxes at once!  I'm in!!!

Okay, so this is a little game about you having someone elses cellphone.  I beat it in a few hours, four maybe, and enjoyed the trip.  Everything you have to do in this game, you do with this cell phone.  You get to break into email accounts, search online registries for sex offenders, and catfish people, all in an attempt to find the ultimate truth.  It's like someone finally based a game off my hobbies.

So, the story is kind of linear, in that you work to unlock new areas of the mystery, piece by piece.  First, you get to play with texts and pictures, then you get enough information to open the email, then you can gather what you need to beat security questions...  I'd say the gameplay is about sifting through information to find what you need to move on.  You also get to talk to the phone owner's friends, and they help to move the plot along, or you can ask them for help if you get stuck.

I say it's linear, but there are actually several branching paths that probably all end up in the same place.  Do you know Telltale games?  Kind of like that... I must admit. I really REALLY enjoyed playing this game.

When I first saw the tag 'Horror', I was a little scared to play this. I'm not a fan of things that scare me, but I managed to get through this and had a blast. *There are a couple jumpscares obviously because why not XD* (I legit flip out at them and tell them to screw off haha)

So in short, Simulacra is about a girl named Anna who has gone missing, and you have to dig through information through her apps, photos, friends, and even people outside of her circle, in order to find out what the hell happened to her.

And I mean you have to dig through a lot of information sometimes.

However, it's not to say that it wasn't fun doing a treasure hunt. Whenever I figured out how to solve one of the tasks based on the information found in different apps, I felt overjoyed. This game makes you really look for the clues where it makes sense.

Also, by the end of the game, I almost felt like I knew the characters. They were very believable, and that's what really connected with me.

Overall, I just love the idea of using solely a phone. It creates a constraint, allowing for so many possibilities and new ways to create and solve puzzles.

I can say that I have only a couple complaints though.

1) When you look through Anna's message history, you come upon these special messages that are in complete disarray. In order to understand what it said, you had to rearrange the words to fix the message. Sometimes, it was just really difficult for me to figure out what that sentence was. I sometimes maybe spent a little too much time and couldn't progress until I figured it out. Most of the messages weren't important enough to do this, except for one. To be honest, I'm probably just not very good at it.

I only really decrypted those messages for my own curiosity, but because they weren't extremely important except for the story-important ones, there was no huge incentive to decode them.

2) While I do like treasure hunting for those sweet juicy clues in the phone data, sometimes the hints are a little too subtle. I'm not extremely great at puzzle games, so I'll miss details, whether they are obvious or not. I think I took a break because I spent so much time trying to figure out something that was so obvious because I simply missed the detail in a sea of texts. Not a big issue, but I just wanted to point that out for the average gamer playing this. I mean I had to look up something once, so it's not bad on my end.

All in all, this game was just amazing, and I look forward to see what's next :D

(Seriously though. I recommend playing this without any spoilers. This was an amazing experience, and it was a good price for such a wonderful story)

This review may contain light spoilers. The TL;DR is that I would recommend it, it's about 3 hours of gameplay, but is quite hand-holdy in parts. Don't go into this expecting a cerebral game where you need to figure everything out for yourself. Also, don't expect the choices the game forces you into making to make any sense, either.

I quite liked it. It's definitely an improvement from the last game, but there are a few things I noticed.
For instance, there's a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the phone's interface through the game, and most notably the 'BUSTED' chatroom, after it's just 2 people left in it, turns into 'BUSTED' is typing, as if the contact name was called 'BUSTED' and this wasn't actually a chatroom.

The knocking, gasps/breathing 'outside' the phone (This game could also be titled "Millennials don't answer the door simulator 2017") were also unneeded. It wasn't that scary and took away from the game, if you're going I was expecting a jump-scare, or some kind of mechanic where I would need to move around my house to avoid various hostile entities from 'getting me' while I solved the phone mystery. 

It was also a bit too linear and railroady for my tastes. The auto-suggestion mechanic needs a lot more work because I felt like I was constantly being railroaded in the dialogue sections down a path that there's no way I (as a person) would have done or said. I wasn't a fan of the two 'supposed-to-lose' parts, either - I spent a good half an hour on one, hunting around and going into every app and going through every bit of information I had so far trying to get more information. 

The story felt very one-track also. If you compared this game to a visual novel, which is pretty much what this game is, a standard VN player would be very dissapointed with the lack of branching paths, different dialogues, and small amount of endings.

I really want to emphasize that the 'free-roam' hunting for information was the best part of this game, and the dialogue elements forcefeeding you stuff you figured out 10 messages ago was the absolute worst. If the devs want to keep on making games like these, the dialog absolutely needs more work. Additionally it seems like the developers really wanted to characterize these people but in the process of haphazardly sprinkling photographs in there were serious inconsistences. Players are going to be combing through this stuff trying to find precious information and the last thing they need is to be misled due to a mistake.

Overall, though, I recommend a buy if this is the sort of game you like. This is a vast improvement upon the last game and I look forward to this studio's next game.

OK, I have just finished one run and I would recommend it!
In shorts,

Goods:
+Lots of contents, even some random guys on Spark, very detailed characterized even for minor characters
+Climax just bumped into at the right moments
+Innovative gameplay rather than just points and clicks
+Real action characters make the game much more immersive
+There are just right amount of minigames beside pure text reading
+Spot on the mentality that people like to check on others' phones and see what're inside, eg. Gallery, videos, etc
+Low price tag!

Bads:
-I can't say Anna is poor at acting, she's good, but she's kind of zoned out during the first second of most of the clips. It looks like that she is thinking what to say then starts acting after one second
-Some unnecessary jumpscares, the script is good, the story is good, come on, you can make the atmosphere scary without cheap jumpscares, make it more subtle, eg. Anna's wallpaper is changing after certain stages, which is spooky and good
-The ending is not so good... The whole process is great but when it comes to the ending... I am ok with the setting but it would be great if the ending part was made longer
-So during the ending part, Taylor is still busy texting you when he's encountering all those shxx? That doesn't make any sense. I understand that there has to be a means to let the players know what is happening. Can't you just make it like Taylor used Facetime with you before all those happened and try to tell the story with videos? As I imagine the scene, I found it very weird that Taylor is dealing with those things and keeps looking at the phone and texts you back and forth. That would be a heavy smartphone addict...
-The story is too long but very linear, which makes replays not quite possible. I want to try the other endings, but it's harsh for me to go for another 4-hour KNOWN adventure. There are many side events to do but the main route is pretty much the same. Maybe you can make it that we start at some certain late points or make the story less linear. We don't like grinding...

That being said, it's still a very great game, I hope there are more localization subtitles coming soon that I can refer to more of my friends from other parts of the world.
I will def buy the next title from Kaigon Games!
Good job! :p

Simulacra is another game within the sara is missing universe. The first game was good but with new additions to a series brings new mechanics and fixes the short commings of the original, does this game do just that? I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The game is very creepy. Now jumpscares are cheap and something I dont really enjoy but the game has ambient sound effects that are very spooky. Sometimes you may hear nocking at a door or a wisper or see the lights flicker in your field of view. Some are not really strong in spooking the player but the sound effects really sell the horror.

      The plot is good. Now this is pretty much a horror thriller game that delves with a deep mystery. The game throws you for many loops making you question who can you trust and how much information you should provide. You never know who is at the other end of that text message you recieved. The further you go the deeper the rabbit hole goes.

        The gameplay is simplistic. A game having a simplistic gameplay is nothing to fear. This is like playing a tale tell game where you get dialogue options but sometimes it effects the response of other players and the ending. There are branching paths but not many to get more than 2ish playthroughs. Still it is good to see that some choices creates a response that effect the story and feels a bit like a genuine response in a hypothetical world.

Con:
      There are some puzzles that are difficult. This game has quite a few moments that test memory and makes you search for clues to progress but some of these clues are very well hidden meaning in order to progress you might need to search the internet for the solution to save the frustration. It is a minor issue but i swear there is this one puzzle i could never solve.

Conclusion:
       In short this game is short but it is a blast to play. The story is creepy with atmoshere and has a great story. If you play the game for just a short ammount of time you will be hooked into finding out the truth. I can not reccomend this game enough for anything curious in the game. It is resonably priced in retrospect to how long the game is.

review_text_raw:
Having played "A Normal Lost Phone", the concept of Simulacra isn't anything new to me, however due to this not being a particularly common way of making a game it is a welcome addition to this genre of sorts. 
Simulacra also comes with a couple of different twists compared to what "A Normal Lost Phone" had so it's not complete copy.

The good:
*You are thrown into an interesting story that you have to go through with the help of strangers. Who should you trust? Who should you be weary of? Wel that's the beauty, you don't know and you have to base your judgements on scraps of information that you can find. The story is definitely one of the highlights of this game.
*The gameplay whilst isn't groundbreaking works well for this game and doesn't propose any friction for the player on how to proceed.
*There's a decent bit of replayability in this game if you want to uncover all of the different paths. They also aren't particularly difficult to reach if given enough thought.

The bad:
*The horror elements of this game... Don't get me wrong, I love myself some horror and this game seems like a good candidate for a bit of it, however the way it is implemented in this specific game is forced and cliche.
Build tension through uneasiness, not through awful jumpscares.
*I don't need to be redirected to a webpage with a Discord server every time I finish the game. It is annoying. If I want to join your Discord Ill find a way to do it without it being showed in my face every time.
*For a game with so many branching I feel like it should've had a save system. If you want to get a specific achievement you are forced to replay the whole game. It is remedied by the faster conversations, but I do not want to listen to the same conversation for 7 times just so I can get an achievement.
*The acting leaves some things to be desired. I understand that this is an indie game but the video segments in this game felt somewhat robotic and lifeless.

Overall, Simulacra is a fun and interesting little game, that will not burn a hole in your wallet and will keep you entertained for a day or two. I think its worth giving a try, if you can stand the occasional jumpscare.

This game is fun and I recommend it -- it's a good way to kill a few hours and is a bargain even at full price. The interface is fun, the mystery is fun, the suspense and creepiness is fun. But there are some not-fun things.

* the jumpscares are just kind of pointless. There's no reason for them to exist, not even within the narrative itself. They ended up making me roll my eyes. The Game's scariest moments are the ones where you feel a slow dread due to the knowledge you've gained

* the story isn't thematically coherent. it doesn't know what it's trying to say. in the end it makes some claim about the fakeness of social media or w/e, but that's not really supported by the rest of the game, which spends a lot more time with the cause and effect of non-social media-related interactions. That makes the denouement feel dissatisfying, as a lot of stuff, like the conflict with the ex-boyfriend or the relationship with the best friend, feel like they could have been replaced with anything else and the story remain intact, which means they're just window dressing and not even that important. It feels disrespectful to the player and to the characters.

* the game has multiple endings but doesn't let you skip ahead when dialogue is playing! This is the most irritating oversight. I ended up pulling up Cheat Engine on second playthroughs so I could turn up the game's speed so I didn't have to wait so long for the chat bubbles to show up. 

* dialogue looks like it was written by non-native English speakers, and I don't just mean text speak, I mean grammar wise it's awkward. Could stand to see some copy editing.

* just generally a lot of interesting concepts and ideas that get raised but not carried out to their full potential. There's a lot here to like, but a lot of misses in execution. I liked the interface messing directly with the player that happens partway through the game, but then nothing ever comes of it. It could have been totally cut from the game and the story would remain unchanged, which is just a bummer.

But those are my gripes, I still had a fun time, so yeah, buy the game!

review_text_raw:
8/10

A very interesting and well done horror game about fiddling with a stranger's phone.

Before Simulacra, the devs made Sara is Missing, a game following the same line (horror game about exploring someone's phone) and, in Simulacra, it's easy to notice how much the game has evolved. While in SIM there were some choices to be made but ultimately they didn't change all that much, in the case of Simulacra it actually changes, with 4 possible different endings depending on what you do during the game.

The game involves talking to people using the phone's messenger app, browsing through other apps, searching for clues and solving some puzzles, while experiencing some creepy things on the way. The story, although somewhat linear (with some differences based on your choices) is interesting and well done. Beating the game once also allows the player to start a new game with faster text speed, which allows for faster playing in order to obtain the different endings.

I think the only two things I feel the game could have done better is that, first, it could have been a little more creepy. Not that it's not creepy - it certainly is - but it's also a little predictable. It could have had some less predictable moments like [spoiler]weird messages showing up in the middle of normal conversations, creepy pictures/videos opening out of nowhere, etc[/spoiler]. The second thing being that there are a few conversations (not many however - just a few) that go on for longer than they need to, sidetracking into subjects that aren't ultimately important when you're trying to find a missing person.

Nonetheless, a very good game and easily worth its asking price.

Also, for anyone who likes this game, I'd also suggest the free game they have released also from the Simulacra series, called "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams".

review_text_raw:
I picked up this game for less than a pack of gums, and it's phenomenal for the price you pay for it. It reminded me of [i] Her Story, [/i] another indie game that was released 2 years before this, so if you liked that, you'll like this as well. It is also similar to [i] Life is Strange, Until Dawn, the Telltale games, Deus Ex Human Revolution, [/i] but this is much lighter and made by a smaller team. 

Unlike the games mentioned earlier, your choices actually matter. If you go in thinking "oh I'm going to play this game and I'll get the good ending and I'll be done with it", then you're wrong. It doesn't work like that, and you can screw up your ending very early on. If [i] Until Dawn [/i] let you save the characters you want by using common sense, Simulacra is not as forgiving. Even if you try to reason with the characters like in [i] Deus Ex, [/i] that's not always going to work. The overall story is entertaining and the characters are great, however, there are some typos, the voice calls are cheesy because they're overdone, being shot in a studio, and the game tries to scare you with its ambience sounds, which aren't connected to the story in any way. There are also some puzzles, some easier, others are harder, which make the game more enjoyable as it's not that linear and actually puts up a challenge.

Overall, I found the game enjoyable. It's replayable, the choices that you make actually have some sort of impact, and the characters are great. There's also a Simulacra spin-off that is free, and there are some sequels. If you didn't get the ending that you wished for, don't feel bad. Some endings are easier to get than others.

It's good but you need to be able to look past 4 big faults to really get into it, as the game can kinda work on moon logic sometimes and it sets you up for failure, not to mention a few other plot holes. 

Also the story is completely railroaded, it has multiple endings but no matter which ending you're going to get, the story and game is pretty much the exact same aside from VERY MINOR character dialog and Ashley not talking to you depending on your choices, until the final scene where it will use choices you made in the past and whether or not you do a specific thing right before the final scene, to determine if Anna and Taylor, the two main characters, are destined to die, or if not, whether or not only one of them will live or if both of them are going to live.

It only branches out and stops being railroaded in the climax and resolution of the game, and since it outright encourages you to replay it to get all the endings, it can't really get away with assuming that people will only play it once, especially since it's extremely easy to fall into the worst ending if you don't do everything right.

Outside of these things, and if you can get past it, this game is good and fun, an intriguing concept and I like Taylor even if he's a total dork. But don't play the phone version as the loops in audio are not as smooth as on the PC version and I experienced a bug that ruined every FMV in the final scene, so you should get it on steam for PC like here.

Went into this completely blind and found it to be a decent game with a slightly above average horror storyline. There are a lot of jump-scare tactics in this visual novel/detective game, many of them unnecessary and overused. The FMVs were done pretty well and the interface is intuitive. The game encourages you to play it again to get different outcomes, but when the first playthrough is over 3 hours I can't be bothered to play a linear story and make sure that I selected certain dialogue options to get all endings/100% achievements.

One thing that I absolutely found hilarious was Greg's voice acting. It's so campy and over-the-top that the first time I heard it I couldn't help but bust out laughing. I'm sure that when he recorded it he had to be clear and precise with his lines, but holy crap it just sounds like a Dragonball Z character powering up for a fight.

I recommend this only because what it does well, it does it *really* well (atmosphere, NPC dialogue, FMV, interface). For the other stuff, it's borderline 80's slasher B-movie status trying to take itself a bit too seriously. There seemed to be some missed opportunities here and gaping plot holes, but I would play another game very similar to this by the same developer with a few new tricks.

Overall, mostly worth your time. Might play Simulacra 2 when I get the chance.

review_text_raw:
The first playthrough is the most fun because you get to explore the game's limits and be a catfishing detective, although the replay value is pretty low for me because then you realize just how short it really is. For $5 though, it is acceptable. The buildup is great and the ending is decent and not what I expected, but pretty original in its own way. I also think they did a great job with the interface and laid out relatively natural methods for you to do your investigating. The journey was definitely better than the destination for me.

I am a fan of interactive storytelling, but the only thing you really feel invested in is finding out what happened to Anna, and if you're sympathetic, wanting to save her, since she is the only character you really get to know through all your interactions and discoveries. The biggest con for me is that the acting and voice acting was okay at best - at times a little too animated/forced - and I felt if there were more development for the characters, the attachment would truly tear us apart as we are forced to make more choices. Also, the creep factor disappeared for me personally once I got through to the ending.

Overall, I do recommend the game, but not very enthusiastically. It was good, but has a lot of potential to be even better.

[h1][b]Genre: Found Phone Adventure/Horror-ish
Time: ~3 hour[/b][/h1]

The player's unnamed character finds a phone on his/her front door, a phone belonging to a woman named Anna. On her phone, there's this weird video of her, making no sense in her speech. After this, you get contacted by different people connected to Anna and the search for what has happened and why the phone landed at your front door can begin.

The phone in itself is quite simple, you've got a phone in front of you, you maneuver it like any other Android phone out there, going through text messages, email, a Tinder clone, a Twitter clone and other apps, in order to find clues as to what has happened. Here and there, you come across a video or a voice message, which also helps to bring the story forward. The only thing I can't really agree on is that people has called it a "horror" game. Maybe I'm just not easily scared, but horror...? Not a chance.

Overall, a pretty good and relaxing game which takes about three hours to complete, but then again... I only finished the game once. There's supposed to be multiple endings and there are some achievements you can hunt through multiple playthroughs just as well.

A short and cheap game that provides a good afternoon's worth of gameplay for your first playthrough. 

The gameplay is well polished and smooth. The music is sometimes a bit too loud for my tastes but it is not bad. The smartphone interface however is very well made and simulates a more comfortable experience swiping and clicking. 

The plot is predictable and voice acting is a bit poor. But the game is rich in story-telling, whether it is relevant to the main questline or not. There is plenty of content lying around that gives the characters life and personality. While the main story is quite linear, many parts of the game can be revealed in a non-linear fashion. The attention to detail in everything in the phone is rather amazing.

The conversation choices are quite interesting and relatable, but sometimes you are forced into conversations that you don't really want to to continue for the sake of plot advancement. 

Overall a very good game well worth more than its full asking price. Will try again.
